forgets to relink the neighbors and leaves the removed node in place
drops an extra node by breaking the head link

questions.explanation: Deletion sets the successor's prev pointer to the predecessor and the predecessor's next pointer to the successor, bypassing the node of value 15. The result is 6 <-> 24 <-> 9 <-> 3; failing to update both directions is the classic bug.
questions.hint: A doubly linked deletion must patch both prev and next of the surrounding nodes.

questions.stem: Solve the problem that follows. A list of 8 nodes indexed 0..7 has its tail linked back to the node at index 1. Using Floyd's slow/fast pointers, at which index do they first meet?

options.misconception: off by one from counting the first repeated visit
reports the tail that closes the cycle instead of the meeting node
reports the cycle entry point rather than the meeting point

questions.explanation: Simulating the pointers: slow advances one node and fast advances two each step until both land on index 7. The meeting point differs from the cycle entry at index 1, which is why confusing the two is a frequent error.

questions.stem: Consider the following question. The values 11, 44, 33, 66, 88, 77, 22 are pushed onto an empty stack in that order, then 4 pop operations are performed. In what order are the values popped?

options.misconception: pops in push order instead of reversing the top k values
treats the stack like a queue and pops the earliest pushed values
reverses the bottom k values instead of the top k

questions.explanation: A stack is last-in first-out, so the 4 pops return the top 4 values in reverse push order: 22, 77, 88, 66. Reading them in push order or taking the bottom of the stack are the queue-style mistakes here.
questions.hint: The most recently pushed value always comes off first.

reverses the first k values when they should keep insertion order
dequeues the last values in push order instead of the first ones

questions.explanation: A queue is first-in first-out, so the 2 removals return the earliest enqueued values in order: 72, 60. Taking the newest values would be stack behavior, not queue behavior.

adds one to each removed value
lists values still in the deque as if they were removed

counts one extra node from the null sentinel children
omits the root or one boundary node

confuses a parent index with a child index

questions.stem: Work from the stated assumptions. A min-heap has array representation 31, 7, 15, 35, 3, 27. After inserting value 13 and sifting up as needed, what is the resulting array?

places the new value at the root without comparing it to its parent
appends the value without restoring the heap order upward

fully sorts the array instead of only building a heap

reports the home bucket and ignores linear probing after a collision
off by one in the probe sequence

off by one in the level count

adds every edge weight instead of selecting the spanning tree
takes the five cheapest edges without skipping cycles
